title: Letter I
focus: ambition and the hunger for discovery

teacherSummary.text: Robert Walton writes to his sister Margaret Saville from St. Petersburg. He is about to sail toward the North Pole, eager to discover a passage and the secret of the magnet, and he describes his self-education and longing for glory.

context.history: Arctic exploration and the search for a Northwest Passage were major public dreams in the early 1800s. Letters were a popular novel form (the epistolary novel).

significance: Walton is Victor's double: an ambitious man willing to risk others for discovery. The frame narrative invites readers to judge whether he will learn from Victor.
discussionQuestions: What do Walton's dreams of the North Pole reveal about his character?
Where does point of view appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with isolation and the need for companionship?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this novel is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Letter I,” how does Shelley show ambition and the hunger for discovery? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the point of view you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Letter I, how does Shelley develop the idea of ambition and the hunger for discovery? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the point of view in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Letter I develops the idea of ambition and the hunger for discovery. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of point of view and foreshadowing shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Letter I (where it begins, turns and ends) and its point of view shape the reader's understanding of ambition and the hunger for discovery. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Letter I suggests about ambition and the hunger for discovery. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's point of view and foreshadowing), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses point of view in Letter I to complicate the reader's understanding of ambition and the hunger for discovery. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Letter I within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of ambition and the hunger for discovery responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Letter I alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of ambition and the hunger for discovery follows or bends those conventions, using the point of view as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Letter I and its treatment of ambition and the hunger for discovery. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's point of view and foreshadowing, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Letter I as evidence for a larger claim about ambition and the hunger for discovery in Frankenstein. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Letter I as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of ambition and the hunger for discovery. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: What do Walton's dreams of the North Pole reveal about his character? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are enticement, fluctuate, effusions, satiate, foretaste. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: “My life might have been passed in ease and luxury; but I preferred glory to every enticement that wealth placed in my path.” In this sentence it means: something that tempts or attracts. Word histories: “fluctuate”: From Latin fluctuare "to move in waves," from fluctus "a wave," from fluere "to flow." For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. Arctic exploration and the search for a Northwest Passage were major public dreams in the early 1800s. Letters were a popular novel form (the epistolary novel). Why does this chapter matter? Walton is Victor's double: an ambitious man willing to risk others for discovery. The frame narrative invites readers to judge whether he will learn from Victor. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for point of view.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. The passage opens: “You will rejoice to hear that no disaster has accompanied the commencement of an enterprise which you have regarded with such evil forebodings.” I stop and ask: what is the author doing here, and how does it connect to ambition and the hunger for discovery? I circle “forebodings”, one of today's words, and ask why the author chose it over a plainer word. When I find point of view, I underline it and write its effect in the margin, then I check my idea against the next sentence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for point of view.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of point of view. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: You will rejoice to hear that no disaster has accompanied the commencement of an enterprise which you have regarded with such evil forebodings. I arrived here yesterday; and my first task is to assure my dear sister of my welfare, and increasing confidence in the success of my undertaking.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Point of view, Foreshadowing, Characterization: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; the app shows the level your teacher assigned (for a 9–10 class, the HS Sophomore prompt reads: Analyze how Letter I develops the idea of ambition and the hunger for discovery. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of point of view and foreshadowing shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to the costs of unchecked ambition? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about ambition and the hunger for discovery, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how point of view shapes ambition and the hunger for discovery. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
